name: YAML
vendor: YAML Language Development Team (open specification at yaml.org)
license: Open specification, free to implement; the spec may be freely copied unmodified
summary: The indentation-based text format behind most cloud configuration: Kubernetes manifests, CI workflows and Compose files.
intro: YAML describes the same data as JSON (mappings, sequences and scalars), but structure comes from indentation and `- ` list markers instead of brackets. Indentation must be spaces; the spec forbids tabs there. Files can carry `#` comments, multi-line strings and several documents separated by `---`. Unquoted values are typed by pattern matching: in YAML 1.2’s recommended core schema, `true` and `false` are booleans, `null` and `~` are null, things that look like numbers are numbers, and everything else is a string. An anchor (`&base`) names a node and an alias (`*base`) repeats it, and tags such as `!!str` or `!!binary` set a type explicitly. Since 1.2, every JSON document is also valid YAML.

The spec lives at yaml.org. The current text is revision 1.2.2 (October 2021), which made no normative changes to YAML 1.2 from 2009. Parsers don’t all follow it: PyYAML, Python’s widely used library, implements YAML 1.1 from 2005, where `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` are booleans and `22:22` is a base-60 integer. There is nothing to buy; YAML is simply the configuration language of Kubernetes manifests, GitHub Actions workflows, Docker Compose files and the Prometheus config file.
strengths: Easy for people to read and edit, with comments and clean multi-line strings, which is why so much configuration uses it
A superset of JSON since 1.2, so tools such as Kubernetes accept either format
Anchors and aliases remove repetition, and one file can hold several documents
The default for Kubernetes, GitHub Actions, Compose and Prometheus, so one skill covers many tools
limits: Unquoted values get guessed types: under YAML 1.1 rules `NO` (Norway’s country code) becomes `false` and `22:22` becomes 1342, and `3.10` is the float 3.1 in any version; quote strings to be safe
Indentation is syntax: one misplaced space silently moves a key to a different parent instead of causing an error
Loaders that honour language tags can run code: PyYAML’s `yaml.load` could call any Python function before 5.1, so use `safe_load` for anything untrusted
Aliases can make a small file expand into a huge structure; the Kubernetes API server’s CVE-2019-11253 was fixed by capping request size and go-yaml’s alias expansion
A long spec with versions that disagree, so the same file can load differently in different parsers

story: Around 2001, Clark Evans and Oren Ben-Kiki were on the SML-DEV mailing list, which was trying to simplify XML, and Ingy döt Net had written a plain-text serialization module for Perl. Together they designed a data language for people first: readability heads their ranked list of goals, with matching the native data structures of dynamic languages third. The first YAML framework was written in Perl in 2001, Ruby shipped one in its core distribution in 2003, and after three years of design work on the yaml-core list, YAML 1.0 was published in January 2004.

YAML 1.1 followed in 2005, with generous implicit typing that read `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` as booleans. Around then the authors noticed that JSON was, by coincidence, almost a subset of YAML. Kyrylo Simonov released PyYAML and LibYAML in 2006, and many other libraries built on them. YAML 1.2 (2009) made YAML a strict superset of JSON and dropped many of the problematic typing rules, but PyYAML, which many other libraries had used as a reference, still implements 1.1. A new design team began meeting in 2020 and published revision 1.2.2 in October 2021.

choices.why: Human readability was the first design goal. Tabs are banned from indentation because different systems treat tabs differently.

YAML wanted to match the native data of dynamic languages without type annotations. In 1.1 the guessing was broad, which caused the Norway problem; 1.2’s core schema narrowed booleans to `true` and `false`.
Repeated nodes are written once and referenced, so YAML can serialize shared objects and graphs, not just trees. Naive expansion of aliases later became a denial-of-service vector.
To be expressive and extensible, a tag can name any type. Libraries such as PyYAML used tags to rebuild arbitrary objects, which is why their default loaders were unsafe for untrusted input.
